new.title: Climb the tower of Sint-Quintinuskathedraal
new.desc: Hasselt's cathedral grew from the 11th to the 18th century, and its tower, which also houses the city carillon, rises high above the Vismarkt and the car-free centre.
new.tip: Go up near sunset, when the light falls across the rooftops towards the Kempen; listen for the carillon on the way down.

new.title: Slip into the walled Begijnhof of Hasselt
new.desc: Behind a wall in the old centre, the beguinage's brick houses still frame a quiet green courtyard. Its church was bombed in 1944 and never rebuilt, and only its outline remains in the grass.
new.tip: Combine it with Z33 and the Jenevermuseum, which are both a few steps away in the same corner of town.

new.title: See what is new at Z33 in the beguinage
new.desc: Z33 is Hasselt's house for contemporary art, design and architecture, with no permanent collection and experimental shows that change every few months. Its modern wing slots boldly into the old brick of the beguinage.
new.tip: Book your slot online before you go and check the programme; the Dusart car park is the closest if you come by car.

new.title: Browse two centuries of style at the Modemuseum
new.desc: Hasselt's fashion museum looks after some 18,000 garments and accessories from 1750 onwards, shown in themed exhibitions instead of a fixed display, which suits a city whose Kapelstraat is a shopping street.
new.tip: Check which exhibition is on before you go, then walk on to the boutiques of Kapelstraat and Aldestraat.

new.title: Find the Virga Jesse statue on Kapelstraat
new.desc: Hidden among the shops of the fashion street, the Virga Jesse basilica holds a medieval Madonna that Hasselt carries through the streets in a huge procession only once every seven years.
new.tip: Step in between shopping stops; the next Virga Jesse feesten are due in 2031, and the whole city decorates for them.

new.title: Trace the lost church of Herkenrode Abbey
new.desc: Founded in 1182 in Kuringen, Herkenrode was one of the great Cistercian abbeys of the Low Countries. Gijs Van Vaerenbergh's Corten steel Clausura now redraws the outline of the abbey church that burned down two centuries ago.
new.tip: The Clausura can be seen free from sunrise to sunset; finish with a Herkenrode beer on the terrace of De Paardenstallen and walk into the De Wijers ponds beyond.

new.title: Hunt down Hasselt's street art
new.desc: More than 60 murals and pieces hide on facades, in alleys and under tunnels around Hasselt, curated by the local street and graphic art collective SAGA.
new.tip: Pick up the free SAGA street art map at Visit Hasselt on Maastrichterstraat, or follow a route in the SAGA app; the corner of Badderijstraat and Zuivelmarkt is a good start.

new.title: Meet the Galloways at Domein Kiewit
new.desc: Hasselt's 130-hectare nature domain sits in the middle of the De Wijers pond landscape, with a city farm opened in 1976, wet meadows with horses, donkeys and Galloway cattle, and walking trails. It turns 50 in 2026.
new.tip: Take the De Lijn bus to the Kiewit Kinderboerderij stop, or cycle via junctions 91 and 95; the Pukkelpop festival grounds are right next door.

new.title: Skate and stroll through Winterland Hasselt
new.desc: Every winter Hasselt sets up one of the biggest Christmas markets in Flanders, with wooden chalets, an ice rink and a Ferris wheel in the city centre.
new.tip: Go early on a weekday evening to avoid the crowds, and warm up with a Hasseltse koffie.

new.title: Join the Jeneverfeesten in October
new.desc: On the third weekend of October around 145,000 people fill Hasselt for the jenever festival, with tastings, music and street theatre across the squares, and the Borrelmanneke statue on Maastrichterstraat pouring jenever instead of water.
new.tip: Saturday is the busiest day; come early to see the Borrelmanneke flowing before the queues build.

new.title: Order a witteke at De Kleine Hal
new.desc: De Kleine Hal claims to be the oldest café in Hasselt and started life in 1836 as a jenever shop. It still pours plenty of local spirits and beers just off the Grote Markt.
new.tip: Ask for a witteke, the local nickname for young Hasselt jenever, and pair it with a Hasselt speculaas.

new.title: Have a drink on the quays of the Kanaalkom
new.desc: The old canal basin around Quartier Bleu and the Blauwe Boulevard has become Hasselt's waterfront, lined with terraces, bars and restaurants overlooking the boats.
new.tip: Grab a seat at Maison Mathis or the Capa rooftop bar before sunset; the Blauwe Boulevard car park is underneath.

new.title: Toast the skyline from the Bon'Air rooftop
new.desc: On the top floor of the Radisson Blu, the Bon'Air sky bar gives a 360 degree view over the cathedral tower and the roofs of Hasselt, and you do not have to be a hotel guest to go up.
new.tip: Order a jenever cocktail and time it for sunset, when the cathedral is lit against the sky.

new.title: Eat a slice of real Limburgse vlaai
new.desc: Since 2024 Limburgse vlaai is an EU-protected regional product of Belgian and Dutch Limburg: a thin yeast-dough base under a thick filling of fruit, rice pudding, custard or crumble, and never any whipped cream.
new.tip: Locals say it should be 'dun van leer en dik van smeer' (thin crust, thick filling); buy a slice fresh at a Hasselt bakery and eat it by hand.

new.title: Climb above the Lommel Sahara
new.desc: In Lommel, zinc smelter fumes and sand digging once left a man-made desert; today 193 hectares of white dunes, pine forest and a lake form part of Nationaal Park Bosland. A 30-metre tower wrapped in rope looks out over it all.
new.tip: Park at sports centre De Soeverein and follow the 6 km orange route past the tower and the forest playground; Café Den Engel is on the way.

new.title: Pause at the German war cemetery in Lommel
new.desc: In the woods of Kattenbos in Lommel lie some 39,000 soldiers, mostly from the Second World War, in the largest German war cemetery in Western Europe outside Germany. A crypt and a basalt crucifixion group overlook the endless rows of crosses.
new.tip: Enter through the crypt for the view over the field; the Huis Over Grenzen peace centre next door tells the story behind the graves.

new.title: Wander the gardens of Alden Biesen in Bilzen
new.desc: The moated castle of Alden Biesen in Rijkhoven, near Bilzen, was for centuries a seat of the Teutonic Order. Its French gardens and English landscape park are open to roam around the buildings.
new.tip: Come on the first weekend of September for Highland Life, Belgium's biggest Scottish festival, with pipe bands, Highland games and a whisky bar.

new.title: Look through the see-through church near Borgloon
new.desc: On a hill among the Haspengouw orchards south of Borgloon stands Reading between the Lines, a church outline made of stacked Corten steel plates by Gijs and Anton Van Vaerenbergh. From some angles it vanishes into the landscape.
new.tip: Walk or cycle there from Borgloon towards the old Roman road; in April the blossom around it makes it extra photogenic.

new.title: Walk the miners' garden city of Eisden
new.desc: In Maasmechelen the Eisden mine built an English-style garden city for its workers from 1911, with tree-lined lanes, big gardens and the Sint-Barbarakerk 'mining cathedral' at its heart. Italian, Greek, Spanish, Turkish and Moroccan miners shaped its mixed community.
new.tip: Follow the heritage walk through the Tuinwijk and look in at the Museum van de Mijnwerkerswoning, a preserved miner's house.

new.title: Tour the old military hospital of Leopoldsburg
new.desc: Leopoldsburg grew up around the army camp of Beverlo, founded in 1835. Its museum fills a former military hospital with a 200-metre corridor and old wards, telling the story of the camp through both world wars.
new.tip: Check opening days on the museum site before you go, as they are limited; the medical wing with its iron lung and operating gear is the highlight.
new.q: Museum Kamp van Beverlo Hechtelsesteenweg Leopoldsburg

new.title: Climb the abbey tower of Sint-Truiden
new.desc: The Romanesque abbey church of Sint-Truiden was torn down in 1798, but its western tower survived. Nearly 200 steps lead to a top with a view over the town and the Haspengouw orchards.
new.tip: Afterwards walk to the Begijnhof, where the church hides medieval wall paintings and a 17th-century Baroque organ.

new.title: Hike up the terril at Thor Park in Genk
new.desc: The old Waterschei coal mine in Genk is now a technology park, but its slag heaps are part of Nationaal Park Hoge Kempen. The Steenmannetjespad climbs the bare northern terril, about 155 metres high, for a wide view.
new.tip: Go at sunset; start at Thor Central, the old mine building that also houses the Mijndepot mining museum.

new.title: Feel the roar at Circuit Zolder
new.desc: Circuit Zolder in Heusden-Zolder hosted the Belgian Formula One Grand Prix ten times and still fills its racing calendar with the 24 Hours of Zolder, truck racing and NASCAR's European series.
new.tip: Pick a race weekend from the circuit's calendar; the 24 Hours and the Historic Grand Prix in August are the most atmospheric.

new.title: Walk to the source of the Voer
new.desc: In the green hills of the Voerstreek, the little river Voer springs up beside the 17th-century Commanderie of Sint-Pieters-Voeren. The Bronnenwandeling around it was voted the prettiest walk in Flanders.
new.tip: Buy fresh fish from the ponds at the Commanderie after the walk; the short loop past the castle suits a half day.

new.title: Watch the birds over the Schulensmeer
new.desc: Between Herk-de-Stad and Lummen, a lake dug in the 1970s doubles as a flood basin for the Demer. When full it is the largest inland water in Flanders, and birdwatchers and anglers flock to its banks.
new.tip: Bring binoculars and walk the dike; in spring rare migrants regularly pull in crowds of birders.

new.title: Taste Ops-Ale at Brouwerij Cornelissen in Opitter
new.desc: In the village of Opitter near Bree, the Cornelissen family brewery has been making beer for generations, including Pax Pils and Ops-Ale since 1937 and the Herkenrode abbey beers.
new.tip: Check the brewery's website for group visits; otherwise order an Ops-Ale or a Bosbier in a café in Opitter or Bree after a ride along the Itterbeek valley.

new.title: Try Achelse Blauwe at Catharinadal in Hamont-Achel
new.desc: The Boonen family farm in Hamont-Achel makes cheese and butter from the milk of rare red-pied MRIJ cows grazing outdoors. Its Achelse Blauwe has been crowned best blue cheese in the world, and its farm plattekaas is an official Flemish regional product.
new.tip: Check the Catharinadal website for where to buy; combine it with a ride through the Kempen heath north of Neerpelt.

new.title: Drink a Bink from Brouwerij Kerkom
new.desc: Bink is the nickname for people from Sint-Truiden and also the beer of Brouwerij Kerkom, a village brewery in the Haspengouw fruit country dating back to 1878 and now run by the De Ranke brewers.
new.tip: Order a Bink Blond or Bruin in a Sint-Truiden café on the Grote Markt, and take home a pot of fruitstroop from the tourist office in the town hall.
